catalog_quote: 2.5.1 Stress Polysyllabic words carry a prominent stress on the first syllable when uttered in iso- lation . In Bunan, the main correlate of stress is pitch, which is illustrated in Figure 31 . ... Conse- quently, stress is not phonemic in Bunan . The trochaic stress pattern discussed above is, however, only attested at the word level, that is in words that are spoken in isolation . When polysyllabic words are uttered in the context of phrases, they follow an iambic stress pattern that is dictated by phrasal intonation . ... Phrasal stress can only be borne by lexical syllables and, accordingly, lies on the stem . The position of phrasal stress depends on the number of syllables that the stem contains . ... new_statements.quote: 2.6. Accent. Accent in Gahri is both phonemic and non-phonemic. Though examples of the phonemic constrast of the accent are attested in a few monosyllabic words only, yet it is very much a part of the sound system in it: e.g. /ló/ south: /lo/ age, year /lá/ goat: /la/ moon. Normally, a monosyllabic words is uttered with a prominent stress accent on it, e.g. /la/ goat, /le/ tongue, /phug/ hole, /du/ cloud. /din/ day, etc. In dissyllabic words, however, the prominent accent is on the initial syllable, if it is close and on the second syllable if both the syllables are open, as in /pum-pa/ shoulder, /wam-pu/ a bear, /lag-thil/ palm, but /khyu-či/ arm, /bo-či/ finger, /cáva/ deer, /si-ga/ saddle, /ku-śu/ a kind of apple, /su-gu/ paper, /phe-ce/ uncle. In polysyllabic words all syllables carry a secondary accent only, as in /te-pań-po/ thumb, /co-bo-ci/ index finger, /la-la-ci/ kid, /ka-ka-ci/ lamb. etc. (not marked).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monosyllables bear a prominent stress accent. In disyllables the prominent accent falls on the first syllable when that syllable is closed, otherwise (both syllables open) on the second syllable. Words of three or more syllables are said to have no single prominent syllable, all syllables carrying only 'secondary accent'. Separately, a marginal lexical accent contrast (acute-marked vs unmarked vowel) distinguishes a few monosyllabic pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author states that in polysyllabic (3+ syllable) words 'all syllables carry a secondary accent only' (i.e. no primary prominence); not marked in his transcription.
new_statements.exceptions: A few monosyllabic minimal pairs distinguished only by 'accent' (ló 'south' vs lo 'age, year'; lá 'goat' vs la 'moon'), which the author calls phonemic accent; one open-open disyllable is written with an accent on the first vowel (/cáva/ 'deer') without comment. No rule given for closed non-initial syllables or for CVC.CVC words beyond the examples pum-pa, wam-pu, lag-thil (all initial-closed).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern isolated words (elicited citation forms) from two Keylong-area speakers; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or of affixed/polymorphemic words.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma describes 'Gahri (Bunan/Punan)' of the lower Bhaga (Gahr) valley, Lahaul, from two speakers of Lower Keylong and Upper Keylong-Guskyar; this is the same language as Glottolog gahr1239 Bunan (ISO bfu), no dialect split involved. Note the LSI-Himachal Pradesh 2023 'Lahauli' chapter is Stod Bhoti, not Bunan, and must not be attached to this key.

readall_conflicts: The one listed open work (Widmer 2014) could not be opened, so nothing new was read from the listed works and the catalog's existing statement (Sharma 1989, sec. 2.6 'Accent', p. 202: monosyllables carry a prominent stress accent; in disyllables the accent falls on the initial syllable if it is closed and on the second if both syllables are open; polysyllables carry only secondary accent; a few monosyllabic minimal pairs treated as phonemic accent) stands as recorded, reading weight-sensitive. There is, however, a documented disagreement waiting in the search-snippet evidence material already held by the project from the 2017 Mouton revision of Widmer's grammar (not a listed item, paywalled): Widmer 2017 sec. 2.5.1 states that polysyllabic words carry a prominent stress on the first syllable when uttered in isolation (trochaic, pitch the main correlate), that stress is not phonemic in Bunan (elsewhere 'only weakly phonemic', with a few minimal pairs such as mik-ti 'tear'), that in phrases polysyllabic words follow an iambic phrase-level pattern with phrasal stress on the second lexical syllable of the stem, that this phrasal stress 'is not sensitive to syllable weight', and that Sharma's monosyllabic 'phonemic accent' pairs (ló/lo, lá/la) contrast in tone/phonation rather than stress.
